First of all she says that she believes her report is not on ethnic cleansing, but she draws the conclusion that the victims were victims in a wide-ranging ethnic cleansing campaign. She also says that she can see a clear picture of ethnic cleansing based on the records on the ARK and Prijedor. She could have included a footnote and let us know, let me know, or the Trial Chamber, where we could see that too. What Dr. Tabeau sees, any demographer has to document in a scholarly work and say on the basis of this, this, and this, I draw such-and-such conclusions and that's why I see it like that. I believe that personal views don't have a scientific basis unless they are well documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the last part of the transcript range that I cited, more precisely I believe it is 36804, lines 1 through 12, Dr. Tabeau went further as to ethnic cleansing and testified as follows: "Yes, I discuss the ethnic cleansing in my report as the context for the Tomasica victims. It is unavoidable to mention the words 'ethnic cleansing' as in my view the deaths, the killings of the Tomasica victims were part of the ethnic cleansing. "And, of course, there is some results, quite some results in my report that support ethnic cleansing considerably. I am speaking of ethnic cleansing from my own experience. It is not the first time that I have been working on the 92 victim, Tomasica victims, also victims from the ARK and Prijedor municipality. I studied other sources of information and made other reports. From my experience and from the work I have done in the past as well, there is quite some support in this report in this work for the ethnic cleansing." From the standpoint of the generally accepted practice of scientific and professional demography, do you consider Dr. Tabeau's discussion of ethnic cleansing to be in line with the accepted terminology and type of review seen in that field?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no definition of ethnic cleansing in demography. What Dr. Tabeau deems to be very important and that she must unavoidably mention ethnic cleansing in her conclusion and that she proved through various reports, while working on Prijedor and the Autonomous Region of Krajina, or the ARK, she has to note in a professionally correct manner in a footnote what are the reports on the basis of which she concludes that this is a case of ethnic cleansing, because a demographer does not have such a definition, and she could then tell us on the basis of this, this, and this, including the experience which Dr. Tabeau says she has. But once again, it has to be founded on a scientific basis. In the report as presented by Dr. Tabeau where she talks about the ethnic cleansing campaign, I did not find a single footnote that would indicate on what basis she concludes that the Tomasica victims are the result of an ethnic cleansing campaign. I also do not know what Dr. Tabeau considers as ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At transcript page 36854, line 20, through 36855, also line 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That can't be right. I believe it's 36855 -- just one moment. It's 36854 and onwards, Dr. Tabeau told us in an answer: "Well, ethnic cleansing is not defined within the field of demography. It is the demography of war, or conflict demography, that has been dealing with issues like ethnic cleansing, among other things." First of all, what is your comment on this.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau says herself that there is no definition of ethnic cleansing in demography, but then she notes that war demography, or demography of war, deals with that. If there is such a discipline of demography as the demography of war, and I don't think that's the case, because Dr. Brunborg in a document of his says that it is about to be constituted. Whether it's being constituted or not, I wouldn't know. But if there is such a thing as demography of war that Dr. Tabeau is aware of and I am not, then the demography of war also must provide some sort of definition of ethnic cleansing, and then this demography of war says we do not apply the legal definition of the United Nations but for us ethnic cleansing represents such and such a thing. And then it may be discussed within demography and agree or disagree whether this definition is good or not. But in any case, it needs to be said what the demography of war implies under this category, ethnic cleansing. If Dr. Tabeau is a war demographer and deals with the demography of war. I believe myself to be no less a demographer of war, but I'm not aware of any definition of the demography of war. It would be nice for me to learn something new or to say, all right, fine, now we have a new definition in demography, or perhaps I might object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the continuation of the pages I cited, 36854, line 20, through 36855, line 20, Dr. Tabeau was asked about which definition of ethnic cleansing she used. And the testimony went like this: "Q. Can you tell us, Doctor, for purposes of your report on Tomasica, what is the definition of ethnic cleansing that you used and had in mind when you drafted the report? "A. I didn't use any particular definition of ethnic cleansing. I interpreted certain demographic distributions as illustrative and indicative of ethnic cleansing in this area, in the area of the ARK and Prijedor in particular." Now before I continue with the rest of the answer, do you have a comment as to what Dr. Tabeau has said thus far?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's really contradictory. First, she says it does not exist in demography as such but it does in the demography of war, but then she says, I didn't use any particular definition but I interpreted distributions. What Dr. Tabeau implies under that I don't know - but specific distributions are made on the basis of ethnicity but there are no special distributions on the basis of ethnic cleansing. You can make a distribution of population based on ethnicity and then draw certain conclusions: this one is rising, this one is falling, this one has remained the same. So as regards this answer of Dr. Tabeau, I don't know how to understand it. It turns out that she used a definition from the demography of war, then she didn't. We know for certain that a definition does not exist in demography and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the continuation of the transcript, we see as follows: "Judge Orie: But, Ms. Tabeau, that requires a certain understanding of what you understand ethnic cleansing to be, and I think that was the question that Mr. Ivetic put to you. "The Witness: So if I may continue then. "Judge Orie: Please. "The Witness: I didn't use any particular definition of ethnic cleansing. I used my own understanding of ethnic cleansing, which I understand as focusing certain actions on a given group of population leading to eradication, largely, of this group from a certain territory, and I saw it from the distributions of the missing persons by ethnicity, by age and sex, which I interpreted as supportive and indicative of ethnic cleansing in the territory of ARK." Professor, from the standpoint of the generally accepted practice of the field of demography as a colleague and fellow demographer, can you comment on these words of Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, someone who is involved in a certain field professionally would deem this answer incomplete and scientifically incorrect. Because Dr. Tabeau says, I didn't use any particular definition, but I used my own understanding. We don't know what one's own understanding is. She had a right to draw such conclusions but she would need to explain that. In my own understanding, ethnic cleansing, it means when you kill only men or only men aged from 5 to 105 or another category. So she had to define what her own understanding was. It wouldn't have been scientifically based because a legal definition in demography is known. But perhaps we could have accepted her understanding if she had provided a definition and relevant argumentation supporting it. But to say that in your expertise, which pretends to be scientifically based, you have your own understanding without providing explanation and arguments and that you only rely on a distribution of some structures without having relevant sources for the distribution, this distribution of the ethnic composition is drawn up by Dr. Tabeau on the basis of one source which is accepted in the scientific world, and that's the population census, and the source that is not accepted anywhere among scientists, and these are electoral roles. So such a distribution on the basis of such sources is not recognised as relevant anywhere among scholars. But if she had explained what her own understanding was and why she thought so we may have agreed, and I may have said all right, that's fine, though I doubt it as the other source which is used as source of the survived population, which is absurd. Electoral roles are not sources from which you can determine what population survived anywhere in the world, so I don't think that this is scientifically acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at Dr. Tabeau's report, it's P7449, page 11 Serbian, page 9 in the English, and it will be the last part of the third paragraph under 2.8 in relation to methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, we should have page 11 in the Serbian and page 9 in the English. I may have misspoken. And we'll need ... one moment, please. We'll need page 11 in the Serbian. We see page 7, I believe, up on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do they correspond, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm trying to -- trying to see which part is being displayed so as to give advice. We need to go -- actually, yes. No, no. No. You can go back to the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what was found in the English on the lower part of the page is found in the upper part in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So the paragraph in question is the third from the top in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the semi-last in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the English starts off with "in this report, in the first place." It should be the third paragraph under the heading 2.8, which I think will be on perhaps the prior page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's indeed not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So the paragraph at issue is the last one on the page in the Serbian. The part I want to focus on will be on the next page in Serbian and it will be the last part of that paragraph up at the top. And it reads as follows: "The methodology is simple but powerful. It's strength relates to using reliable sources and to benefitting from matching and merging of the various sources at the individual record level. When matching and merging of the source, I always pay particular attention to the identification and elimination of duplicates." Professor, can you comment as to this part of Dr. Tabeau's report.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The methodology is simple but powerful. What does powerful methodology mean? You have scientific and non-scientific methodology. In scientific research and methodology, there is nothing that's powerful. This something that is beyond the scientific or its more scientific than the scientific method. So it's not comprehensible what powerful methodology is. There's no explanation. But based on all the procedures used, it can be noted that this methodology is special and does not comport with scientific methodology. This profitable methodology is not practiced, not applied in the scientific world, as far as I know, because it represents an adaptation of some methodological solutions which are applied in scientific work to the needs of one's own research. Therefore, when you say that the methodology is simple but profitable without explaining what the profitable part would mean, this is just a pure phrase or terminology that has no meaning. I underline it does not have any significance without an explanation, unless one understands it as selecting what you need and choosing what you need for your own research purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to 1D6187, and this will be an article published by Dr. Tabeau from 2005. And it will be on page 20 in the Serbian and page 22 in the English language. And it will be in the middle of the page in the English, and I think it's the fifth paragraph up from the bottom of the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Just one minor point, Your Honour. Counsel represented this as an article by Dr. Tabeau. I believe it's an article -- it's co-authored by Dr. Tabeau, and I just think that should be on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it will be in the middle of the page of the B/C/S, starting [B/C/S spoken], and I'll --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I cannot follow, which paragraph is it in the Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The fifth paragraph up from the top which should be at approximately the middle of the page which starts out [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'll read. "International organisations operating in Bosnia, such as, for example, ICRC, ICMP, and UNHCR, made considerable contributions to the process of collecting information about war-time missing persons, deaths, identification of victims, and internal and external migration. The mandates of these organisations have, however, other major objectives than producing statistical information about casualties of war. Their contributions can therefore not be seen as a substitute of the outcomes of regular statistical activities normally conducted in peacetime." Then the next paragraph, it starts: "The contributions of (local and international) non-governmental organisations operating in Bosnia, being meaningful and important, can for the same reasons not be considered as replacements for regular statistics." What do you have to say about what is written in this article co-authored by Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau knows exactly what can and what cannot be considered as valid official data in demography or mortality or in official documents. In this study of hers, which is intended for the broader professional public, she correctly delineates the point of I know what should be done, and that these were the things that the international organisations did who don't usually do this kind of work. So in the analysis that I looked at, she does not inform any Trial Chamber about this, and she does not say: These sources of data that I acquired from non-governmental organisations do not substitute the work of regular statistical services because they would result in such-and-such a problem. So this approach would be a kind of caution about the overall quality of the expertise that is being done. If it cannot be measured with official statistical sources of data, then there must be some kind of observation about the quality of the expertise that you are producing. In many expert reports, including this one, Dr. Tabeau says that the objective is to present accurate data. However, she does not have a source for accurate data.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 4 in the same work in Serbian and in English, and it will be, I believe, at the middle of the page in both. So it's the middle paragraph that in Serbian begins, "[Interpretation] Note that our research results ..." [In English] And in English I will continue reading: "Note that our research results were obtained from a project somewhat different from the usual statistical and academic work. Our perspective was in line with that of expert reports submitted to the Trial Chambers at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) as part of the (prosecution) evidence. The goal of such reports is to provide the Chambers with high-standard war-related population statistics satisfying the requirement of being 'beyond a reasonable doubt' and consistent with the framework of the international humanitarian law." Professor, from the standpoint of the generally accepted practice of professional demographic science, what comment do you have on this approach as stated in this article co-authored by Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, quite rightly, says that this is not in accordance with the usual academic work without explaining what it's supposed to be in accordance with. Unless we accept as an explanation that their perspective is in keeping with the -- is in line with that of the Trial Chambers at the International Criminal Tribunal or the Prosecution, what would be that perspective in line with the Prosecution if it deviates from customary professional procedures? I mean, we would need an explanation for that. She then notes that the research is not in line with academic work and then that the sources of data are not the customary sources used in research that is in line with academic work and that these are organisations whose results are not even close to official results. I don't know exactly which words she used. How can then the conclusion be made that the results offered to the Prosecution are of high quality which satisfy criteria of the Tribunal and are in accordance with international criminal law? In my deep conviction, the criteria of the court, and I assume of the Prosecution as well, can only be satisfied by the criteria and results that are scientifically founded, methodology that is applied in scientific academic research. If Dr. Tabeau does believe that this is in line with international humanitarian law, then again she would need to footnote that and say that international humanitarian law perhaps recognises the methodology that one would devise oneself and that that can deviate from all kinds of things, but then I believe that in that case that would be proper and correct. I don't know -- of course, I don't claim to know everything, but I don't know that international humanitarian law insists on getting reports that deviate from scientific professional conditions needed for such a report to be acceptable. I don't know about the court. I mean, I don't know. And perhaps Dr. Tabeau does know that and perhaps she could explain this to us how this special methodology, which is not in line with the science, has significance for the Tribunal and the Prosecution, or how, on the basis of special methodology, one would acquire statistical data of high quality. Also, it is very interesting - I would like to know - for example, had Dr. Tabeau put in a footnote explaining what it is that would satisfy the criteria of the Tribunal. What is it that would satisfy the Court's criteria? There is a partial explanation for that in Srebrenica. I described that in my own report. In that case it is considered that a large number, even though the Court never says that anywhere, is one of the elements to satisfy the criteria of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following. A small portion was read, and you commented in a long answer on that. What conclusions does Dr. Tabeau draw from the fact that the usual statistical academic work could not be applied? What triggers that in her mind in this paragraph; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She makes a distinction between what is applied in science and what is applied in court, and she says properly that in science such and such a thing and such and such sources. However, our expert report was done from the perspective in accordance with such and such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What she says you then should do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She doesn't say anything in this report about what should be done. She, however, presents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the article, I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the article that she published in a professional publication, she does not say what should be done. If I may explain it briefly. She says we're going to present the war-time victims. It should be like this, but we're actually doing it like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll phrase the question in a different way. What I read in this report immediately following the portion that was read to you, she writes, or they write: "The first prerequisite implies that questionable, deficient, incomplete sources and/or individual death causes [sic] are excluded from our statistics." Cases. Where I said "causes" I should have read "cases." I understand that to be that if you are using this unusual method that you should be very careful in excluding sources which are, as she writes, deficient, incomplete. That's apparently the conclusion she draws. Is that something you would consider wise to do and acceptable to do under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. First of all, these are sources that are never used in the scientific research for what Dr. Tabeau is writing. And then she says we are using those that are not used, but the first preconditions in those which are usually not used for scientific research would be to exclude duplicates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd say that questionable, deficient and incomplete sources, you consider that a reference to duplicates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What is meant are the insufficient, questionable, incomplete sources from the Red Cross, ICMP, and so on, which also contain, among other things, duplicates, and then those sources that are used by the doctor are verified, they're checked. And then when you find duplicates, because there were cases that in the Red Cross or in several sources you have one person appearing a number of times because it was reported by different relatives, so when you take a source where a same person is found to have been reported three or five times, that would be excluded and leave just one such report and not five. So that is their procedure regarding the incomplete sources which is not usually applied in scientific research in demography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to your report, 1D6184, and page 14 in the English and page 18 in the Serbian and paragraph number 35 of the same. In paragraph 35, you pose a question: "What is the specialist and scientific significance and what is the real value of results obtained in research different from the usual, statistical, and academic work without being comparable to any methodologically, scientific, and specialist procedure recognised in statistical and demographic research in the world?" What do you mean here? How would you answer?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that Dr. Tabeau was obliged to explain this. Since Dr. Tabeau did not explain that, I am putting this question to the Trial Chamber, even though I don't have a right to that. However, my answer to that question would be that all the findings would be pretty suspect, that they are not scientifically grounded, and that Dr. Tabeau explains this nicely in her work but not in the report. Because I really don't know, if it's only Dr. Tabeau who asserts that her work is sound in the report to the Chamber but that it is not done according to the customary rules, I don't know to what extent this is acceptable because it's not scientifically grounded. So I think that the answer to that is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, in the next paragraph you pose a second question: "To what extent does the expert's project, being somewhat different from the usual statistical and academic work contribute to misinformation?" Do you have an opinion as to the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. Dr. Tabeau always says there are some differences. That can mean that there are drastic or minimal differences, that they can be neglected or not. I don't believe that there are negligible differences. I believe that there are substantial, drastic differences. And if such differences exist in the opinion of Dr. Tabeau, and if they're just slight, or if she believes that they are not just slight, then she should answer the question of how much do they contribute to correct, accurate, information of the Trial Chamber, or to the misinformation of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to put matters very clear. Your answer, if I understand you well, is that this project is considerably contributing to misinformation. Is that how I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would really need to look at all the projects now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat her last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to step away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you come a little bit further away from the microphone. That's what the interpreters ask. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the project did contribute to misinformation, and it's not only the Tomasica project but also about the change of the ethnic structure, the ascertaining of the number of dead, and warranting that they are dead, and so on and so forth, because it is founded on data sources which, had they been professionally done and had it not been aspired to a large number but to things that could be proven reliably and definitely, the findings would have been much more acceptable as such. However, the projects or the reports make it evident that the accent was on the number, on presenting the highest possible number. I cannot claim that certain sections in some reports are not acceptable, but I can assert with a great degree of certainty that some parts from a large number of the expert reports are absolutely unacceptable in the methodological sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 37, Professor, you pose a third question, which I will not read but we have before us. What, if anything, would you like to say in regards to this question posed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere - and I mean nowhere - does Dr. Tabeau in this report, and in the majority of others, give her opinion on the degree of the reliability of the results. If you use unusual or uncommon sources, then it would be logical to talk about the degree of reliability as well, which is arrived at on the basis of an assessment of the sources that you are using. If Dr. Tabeau did assess the sources that she was using, trying to be professional, and she could say there are many empty fields or some data is still missing, she never expresses that in the way that a demographer or a statistics expert would say. There are some places where she would say 1.300-odd pieces of information are not correct, but then at the end of it all she concludes that all of that is acceptable. In this report, for example, she says the Red Cross does have some omissions, there are still some empty fields. The Prijedor Book of the Dead has many more failings, and then she lists them saying that almost a half of the persons registered in the Prijedor Book of the Dead, I think it's about half, are not given the place of death, if I'm not mistaken. I can check that. But as I said, when you merge those two sources, then they are acceptable. How can you get one good source from two bad ones? All I can conclude is it can happen because Dr. Tabeau did the matching. What I didn't find in the Prijedor Book of the Dead, I'm going to find in the records of the Red Cross, and that's how we get to that. So again, we come to the problem of not knowing how she did the matching. She does not say in any of the reports: This is the criteria we used to move things, to match things, and then these three criteria or these five criteria. In this report she says: According to the methodology used in the case of Srebrenica, which means that 72 criteria were used, if you use 72 criteria, you can match whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the criteria. I would like, first of all, to have you explain to us what you mean when you say "degree of reliability," and what is, in the generally accepted field of demographic work, how is that degree of reliability usually expressed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could think over the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that we take a break first. And could you please give focused answers rather than very lengthy answers which often move away from what is really asked. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is there any way that you could keep the witness a bit closer to your questions, because the question you are putting to her now is -- is similar to the previous question where apparently no answer was given which would satisfy you. Therefore, the balance between the length of the questions and the length of the answers seems not to be optimal. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber was informed that you would like to raise a procedural matter. Can we deal with it in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I advised my colleagues from the Defence that I wanted to raise this issue at this juncture because I considered that it would not implications for the timing of the rest of the week and was also a matter that should be raised as soon as possible in our ongoing efforts to expeditiously conclude the case, and that is the Trial Chamber's invitation in its recent decisions on the bar table motions, specifically in the ninth decision at paragraph 14, to make submissions on the timing of the tendered documents in the context of the bar table motions. Now, I note preliminarily that this submission is about the issue of timing, not about the appropriateness or even necessity of the admission of the documents that have been tendered by the Defence -- by the Prosecution in order to contextualise or clarify or that are otherwise intimately related to a document tendered by the Defence. And we consider that given the practice in this case in related matters, and in particular the message from the Court in its recent decisions, that the issues seem to be about timing and not about the issue of admissibility per se. We consider that the answer to that question lies in the distinction between rebuttal and this particular process, irrespective of the fact that both may be vehicles for the admission of evidence that may ultimately shed light on the probative value to be accorded documents tendered by the Defence. Thus, rebuttal is and refers to evidence introduced by one party to contract or nullify the evidence introduced by another. Now, that is necessarily a sequential process; that is, you can't rebut evidence until it's admitted. And as we all know, the process of evidence admission takes place in a sequential basis pursuant to defined aspects or phases of the case. Now that is different from the process of admitting documents because that process, the question of considering the admissibility of a document and the possible admission of related documents, necessarily involves the consideration of other documents that bear on the tendered doc, and that is something that the Trial Chamber itself has acknowledged in the eighth and ninth bar table motions when it made reference to the factors that it was considering in connection with the admissibility of those documents; their probative value, their reliability, and so on. I would also note that this was the approach that was adopted and implemented by the Karadzic chamber when it considered Defence bar table motions. That is, it considered the submissions of the Prosecution in connection with the -- with the issue of other contextualising, clarifying, or otherwise intimately related documents to the documents submitted by the Defence, and in many cases it denied admission of the documents tendered by the Defence on that basis but in at least one case it admitted the tendered Defence document along with a couple of contextualising documents submitted by the Prosecution. In short, Your Honours, we consider that the process of evidence admission is -- which includes consideration of other documents apart from the specific tendered document, and the possible admission of those intimately related documents, is part of an integral and compartmentalised process that is separate from rebuttal despite the fact that they both are vehicles for admission. And I would say in that regard that if the Trial Chamber were to find that the documents the Prosecution has submitted were not related to the Defence tendered documents in that fashion, then those documents would be suitable instead for rebuttal. And finally I would make this plea to the Chamber, and that is to ask the Trial Chamber to do its utmost to complete its decisions on the bar table submissions at the earliest possible opportunity and if at all possible before the conclusion or before the commencement of the week of the 30th, recognising that -- that -- that we're all pressed for resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The 30th of May. Did I say April? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you didn't say a month. You didn't give a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm relating that, of course, to the end of presentation of Defence evidence. I think it's clear that that would result in the greatest possible efficiency and certainty for the parties and avoid the risk that we may found ourselves litigating matters or even deciding matters related to evidence as we approach the very last parts of the case related to the submission of the final brief. So I thank you for your time, Your Honours, and hope you understand why the Prosecution chose to raise this matter at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think I will not surprise anyone by saying I wasn't exactly prepared to respond today to these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one expects you to immediately respond to something not earlier announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So I would defer then, and I'll try to, at the earliest possible, perhaps even by the end of the week, come back with something perhaps in writing which would then save us time from the court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which also gives us an opportunity to carefully read your submissions, Mr. Tieger, because I think it's a rather delicate line between related to the documents or clarifying, and then the timing, whether it should be done now or at the rebuttal phase, that apparently is the issue the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. And if I could identified a bright line along that spectrum, I would have. I certainly -- I would agree that there are documents that clearly fall on one end of the spectrum and the other end. Where those two merge is a little bit more difficult and nuanced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it to that for the time being. Perhaps you may revisit the matter. And I think since we are sitting on Thursday and not on Friday, perhaps it would be good if you briefly respond -- if the Defence would briefly respond by Thursday so that we can further consider the matter. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps a very practical matter. I think for interpretation purposes, Mr. Segers was scheduled for this Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we should stick to that. There is a fair chance, if I look at all the estimates now, that we'll not conclude to hear the evidence of Ms. Radovanovic this week. So therefore, we should continue with Mr. Segers and interrupt hearing the evidence of Ms. Radovanovic on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. And my understanding is that the Dutch language translators are available from the first thing on Thursday, so our plan was to start with him, complete him and get him on his way, and resume with Professor Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask the parties, and I'm already addressing the Prosecution as well, to try to keep the witness on track in responding to the questions rather than to give long explanations which go further and further away from what was asked. I'm also saying this, Mr. File, because I saw that there was an extended estimate of time, and please reconsider whether you can reduce it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do everything to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I have been asked to try to ask you to keep your answers as short and concise as possible so that we can complete the remaining portions of your testimony. In that regard, let me try to shorten the question that I posed before the break and just simply ask you: In what manner is degree of reliability usually expressed in demographic work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, by judging the quality of the sources you are using and then the demographic indicators based on which you express what you found, and it's known exactly what's the demographic indicator for mortality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in what format is degree of reliability reported in demographic work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a numerical format, which you may later describe and say the error is such and such, I accept or I do not. And, of course, the errors depend on the characteristics. And the source is -- the more valid, the fewer errors it contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At transcript page 36819, line 22, to 36822, line 14, Dr. Tabeau testified about this topic. We'll take the items of the testimony one by one to try to keep things as concise as possible. The first question posed to Dr. Tabeau and her answers are as follows: "Q. Wouldn't it be accepted practice in the field of demography to assign a grade or reliability factor to a particular source that is being used and to report the same in your demography report? "A. Yes, Mr. Ivetic. Absolutely." And in relation to this part, Professor, do you agree with Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does Dr. Tabeau's Tomasica report give any such grade or degree of reliability for all the sources she used in her report as you would except to see from a colleague engaged in the field of demography?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. She mostly describes the insufficiencies of a certain source; for example, the Book of Dead from Prijedor. And, for example, with regard to ICRC, she says there are still many shortcomings and some errors do occur. So she does not provide that as usual. I cannot say that she doesn't mention certain numbers with regard to the Prijedor Book of Dead, but she does not provide a final assessment but she just says overall the source may be accepted, or all in all when we combine these two sources then they may be accepted. In scientific demographics "overall" or "all in all" is not an acceptable description.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we continue with Dr. Tabeau's testimony, what is accepted in demographic studies? What degree of reliability is required for a work to be deemed acceptable for scientific work? What degree of reliability as to a source is required?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The percentage of error within a source that is later published may be between 2 and 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the continuation of Dr. Tabeau's testimony in the transcript range that I read out earlier, the second -- the next question posed was as follows: "Q. And so could you please help me then why are you unable to provide such a grade or reliability factor for the data from ICMP demographically speaking? "A. Yes, for the simple reason that I don't rely on this source. When I discussed the disappearance information of the victims, I used mainly the ICRC records in combination with the records from the Book of Missing, Prijedor Book of Missing, and I'm not using basically the ICMP disappearance information." Do you have a comment as to this, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She could have provided an assessment of ICRC, perhaps not a descriptive one as "all in all it's good" and "I accept it as such." She provides a descriptive assessment for 2005 by saying that from 2000 and something until 2013, not the number of the missing, but she doesn't say in 2005 there are still some fields that are missing -- I am paraphrasing now, I don't know how to quote it exactly but I can read the quotation if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that if need be. For now, I'd like to stick to the development of Dr. Tabeau's answers. In the next question posed to Dr. Tabeau in that transcript's range I read earlier read as follows: "Q. Are you in a position to report a grade or reliability factor for these other sources that you did rely upon? "A. Well, it depends on what you want me to provide. If you want a number, a single number, then I don't have such a number. But I do have an opinion about the reliability of both ICRC and the Prijedor Book of Missing. I have been working with ICRC, in particular, for many years, and several times I studied the reliability of this list and assessed the list as very reliable, as a matter of fact, although not free of certain deficiencies like gaps in the data or incorrect dates of birth, for example, victims. These kind of issues are there, of course." Professor, what would you have to say in comment to this testimony of Dr. Tabeau, especially that the reliability factor she can't express any number?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The degree of reliability can always be expressed numerically. But when Dr. Tabeau says I don't have a number but I have an opinion, what does she base her opinion on if it's not on some relative ratio of errors in a specific source? If she says there are still certain shortcomings, also that is unacceptable. Are these shortcomings 1 per cent, 30 per cent, or what? It means that you are basing your opinion on the reliability based on the parameters that you use to evaluate a specific source.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the continuation of Dr. Tabeau's testimony in the stated transcript range, the testimony developed as follows: "Q. Okay. You've told us about the ICRC list. What about the other sources you use? Can you give us an assessment in demographic terms of the quality or reliability factor of the other sources you use for the Tomasica report? "A. The most important source is, of course, the ICMP list of DNA matched note officials, and I certainly have a very high opinion about the ICMP records, and this is a reliable list that I have no reasons to doubt. "ICMP have been used -- again many times. I have used the ICMP list many times in various cases. I unfortunately have to mention Srebrenica again, Mr. Ivetic, as it was the most substantial case in which these records were used, but also in other cases. I used the Prijedor Book of Missing which is a sources made locally in the Prijedor municipality. This source is less reliable than the ICRC list, yet it highly overlaps with the ICRC list; however, there are many more deficiencies in the Prijedor Book of Missing like missing pieces of information or errors in the date of birth. "I studied also the 1991 census which I assessed several times also during other projects presented in this case about which I testified in November 2013. I used the integrated mortality database which was a source for cross-referencing the records of the missing and checking whether the reporting of the disappearance is consistently reported there as well and to exclude the possibility that someone has survived Tomasica, but they didn't, or were confirmed dead." "Q. What reliability factor? You told me what you use, I believe, in your report. I'm asking for a reliability factor for, for instance, the 1991 census and the integrated mortality database which you just mentioned? Could you please answer that question." And the answer of Dr. Tabeau was: "Well, I again cannot give you a single number on the scale from one to ten, for example, because I don't have such a scale. But as I'm saying, census, for example, 1991 census, even though it has its problems, it's a very useful source for checking -- improving the validity of the reporting by other sources. Well, we as the demographic unit invested a lot of time and effort to eliminate mistakes from the census and improve the reporting of the names in the census. It took us several years until we established a version that could be reliably used in our work, and honestly I believe it is a very reliable source of information, very reliable source of information that proved to be helping me to make decisions about many things, like, you know, matching on the first place, consistency of lists, places of residence, places of disappearance, ethnicity, age, many, many, many, many aspects that I studied in my reports, integrated database is a very large database that is a compilation of several sources -- "Q. How reliable is it, ma'am? "A. In my eyes, very reliable." Professor, as a practitioner in the field of demography, what if anything do you have to say about the testimony and answers of Dr. Tabeau in this section I've just read?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For most of the explanation, Dr. Tabeau is telling you about the population census in 1991, and she says that it's reliable and I agree with her absolutely. It is highly reliable because it's official data, and I'm sure that the institution took care about the range of error. However, the name, surname, and father's name are not statistical data, and Dr. Tabeau says that they lost time and time to correct that statistical data. There is no other source which we could refer to so that we could say the corrections were well made or were not well made, but it could have been said that in the census we corrected 40 per cent of names, last names, father's names, some where these were just typing errors, some where we had completely different names, and so on and so forth. One must keep in mind that the population census was done in the Latin script and the Cyrillic script, so the translation from Cyrillic into Latin script can result in errors. So professionally, it would be correct to say we corrected 30 per cent, 50 per cent, 60 per cent, 2 per cent of names and surnames. Everything else other than names are facts indicating that the census is a reliable source. But the -- Dr. Tabeau used the census to compare data from the Red Cross. For example, the person that she found in the Red Cross records, she would check back to see if they were in the census, and so in the case of Srebrenica they used that to consider -- or to establish that the persons that they believed to be victims in Srebrenica were not fictitious persons and they really did exist. I don't know how they did this matching. I'm not going to go into that. I saw the table. But I don't know what it was they took into account in the matching. But again, it would have been professionally correct for them to say: Okay. I matched this list according to this criteria, that criteria, and other criteria. In Srebrenica we saw that they compared the Red Cross with the population census, and they used this criteria: First name, last name, father's name, and the date of birth, the rate of matching was 16 per cent. And this is in relation to the Red Cross, which has 22.000 entries for missing persons. What Dr. Tabeau took from the population census, let's say the ethnicity, because no other sources contain the ethnicity, so again she takes it again according to the decisions used in matching. We used -- we saw how she used it in that particular graph, how she matched the ethnicity. As for what she says, that she could check the place of disappearance in the census, there is no information in the population census about the place of disappearance. The population records the living.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, if I could ask you very briefly, does a professional a demographer and statistician keep a record of what matching keys or criteria are used, and if so how would this be reported in relation to the scientific research or report that is authored resulting from the matching inquiry?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In professional work, this is done. Not how, but which. We know what matching is and what this implies, that something is matched. However, you must note the criteria that were applied. Dr. Tabeau says that in the mortality database there is no chart of that. So how is the matching done if you don't know what criteria you are using? You devise a criterion which you believe is good and which you believe will show you with high degree of probability that -- that's the right person, and that's the criterion you start with. And then when you get results on the basis of that criterion, you can then say: Okay. I got 16 per cent. I don't like 16 per cent. And then I can shorten the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question was whether a record would be kept professionally. You've answered that question already in the first two lines. I'm also looking at the clock, Mr. Ivetic.
